_about: The spoken script, in the reference film's pattern: second-person present-tense narration in short beats, in-scene dialogue, deliberate pauses. 'who' is 'narrator' or a cast id (src/film/generic/cast.ts). 'pause' = silence after the line, in seconds (default 0.5 after narration, 0.35 after dialogue). Facts follow docs/storyboard.md. Build the audio with scripts/build-audio.py.

1.text: You open your eyes. Smoke. Straw. Cold.

2.text: By tonight, you'll reap another man's harvest,
and see what happens to a man who said no.

3.text: The other half of the bed is already cold.
She rose before you. She always does.

4.text: On the lord's rolls, you have a name. Walter atte Brook.
Your land, your labour, even your daughters' marriages answer to one man.

5.text: Look around. Oak posts. Hazel. Mud.
The smoke finds its own way out, through the thatch.

6.text: Alice is back from the well.
She coaxes last night's embers back to life.

7.text: Joan, fifteen. Already eyeing a boy.
Little Agnes. And the baby, who coughed half the night.
Two more lie in the churchyard.

8.text: Breakfast. Dark bread and weak ale.
Everyone drinks ale. Even the children.
Add hose, shoes and a hood. You're dressed.

9.text: Today. And Walter, your pig was in the lord's barley again.
Gilbert is the reeve. A villein like you, driving his own neighbours.

10.text: Outside, the village is waking up.
One muddy street. Every family has a croft, a pig, and one grudge.

11.text: Your day is measured by the sun, and the church bell.

12.text: Your grain must be ground at the lord's mill.
One scoop for you, and one for me.
The miller takes his toll. And probably a little more.

13.text: So you keep a hand-quern hidden under the straw.
Grinding at home is forbidden. At St Albans, an abbot will pave his parlour with confiscated querns.
And in 1381, rebels will rip them up.

14.text: Those are the lord's pigeons. Only the lord may keep doves.
They eat your seed corn. You may not touch them.

15.text: Every man over twelve is in a tithing. Ten neighbours, answerable for each other.

16.text: You may never speak a word to him.
But you will feel him every hour of your life.

17.text: At the well, Joan and the miller's boy are very much not talking.

18.text: Then you see it. Your land.
Not one farm. About thirty narrow strips, scattered across vast unfenced fields.

19.text: Year after year, the plough heaps each strip into a ridge.

20.text: To the lord's corn! All of you!
The hayward is calling the village to work.

21.text: Everyone but your wife must reap the lord's field first.

22.text: Grab a fistful. Cut. Lay it down. Step.

23.text: Joan binds the sheaves. Hugh chases crows and hauls water.
At nine, he's already a labourer.

24.text: Every tenth sheaf is marked and left standing.

25.text: Five years ago, it rained all summer.
Seed rotted. Prices soared. People ate their seed corn, then their horses.
That winter, you buried a child.

26.text: And now, a plague on the cattle. Oxen are dying across England.
Your plough team can't pull. And the lord's ploughing comes first.

27.text: At noon, the lord feeds his reapers. Bread. Cheese. Maybe herring.
On a wet boon, there's ale.

28.text: No doctor. Just linen and prayer. The coroners' rolls are full of this.

29.text: By mid-afternoon, a dark line of cloud.
Your own wheat stands ripe, on the far side of the field.

30.text: A bush on a pole means Matilda has brewed.
Fresh brewed! Come and get it!
Ale sours in days, so women brew constantly.
The ale-tasters fine anything thin, or overpriced.

31.text: In church, the wall shows devils dragging sinners into a monster's mouth.
You can't read. You don't need to.

32.text: Ah, Walter. Don't forget the tithe.
Your priest takes a tenth of your grain, your lambs, even your eggs.

33.text: Father, I want to marry him.
First, you must pay the lord merchet: a fine for permission to marry.
Some lords even fined unwed mothers.

34.text: A hare bolts from the stubble.
Catch it, and you'll be fined.

35.text: Even the king reaches this far.
His tax men value your pots and animals.
That sack. For the king's army.
His purveyors take grain for his wars, and pay late, or never.

36.text: News! The Scots are burning the north! And the king is feuding with his barons!
It all feels very far away.

37.text: The real dangers here are ordinary. Open wells. Ditches. Cooking fires. Carts.
Coroners recorded toddlers drowning while their parents worked the harvest.

38.text: Peasants buy, sell and lease land, and the court records every deal.

39.text: On the way home, you pass John Cok's house.
His byre is empty. His cow is gone.
And John won't meet your eye.

40.text: Three weeks ago, on a boon day, John reaped his own corn instead.
My corn was rotting. What was I to do?

41.text: The court fined him. He couldn't pay.
So the lord's men took his cow, until he pays.

42.text: Walter atte Brook. His pig, in the lord's barley.
But I didn't even see it!
Your own neighbours sit as jurors. And you can't pay.

43.text: If you fall sick, the work is still owed.
Send a son. Hire a man. Or pay.
And when you die, the lord takes your best beast. The priest, your second.

44.text: But the court names you, and orders your family to bring you back.
Survive a year and a day in a chartered town, and you might be free.

45.text: Our grandfathers were free men! It's in the Domesday Book!
They searched for proof, refused services together, and sued their lords.

46.text: Released at last, you run to your own strip.
You reap until you can't see your hands.
Half of it is still standing.

47.text: Next door, Emma lost her husband last winter. She kept his land.
Mistress Emma. Have you thought about remarrying?
Every day, sir. Every day you ask.

48.text: Hot to the touch. And no physician comes to a villein's cottage.
Alice tries a herb. A charm. A saint's name.

49.text: Before dark, Hugh pens your sheep on the lord's land.
Because their dung manures his fields. Not ours.

50.text: Supper is pottage. Peas, beans, leeks and oats, stewed for hours.
No potatoes. No tomatoes. Not for centuries.

51.text: Alice spins wool by firelight, one eye on the cradle.
Her hands haven't stopped since before dawn.

52.text: Pater Noster, qui es in caelis.
Words you can't fully translate, for a child you can't heal.

53.text: Your wheat is still in the field. Nothing to do but wait for dawn.

54.text: Alice banks the fire under ash.

55.text: Twenty-eight years from tonight, a plague will kill perhaps half of England.
Labour will become precious. And men like you will start to say no.

56.text: You'll leave no portrait. No letter. Maybe one line in a court roll.
But walk across an English field today, and look closely.
The ridges and furrows you ploughed are still there.
So, could you have survived one day as Walter?
